claim: Numerous brain areas, including the hippocampus, have been implicated in representing space and facilitating navigation.
source: Numerous brain areas, including the hippocampus (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Rosenbaum et al., 2004; Spiers and Maguire, 2006; Bird and Burgess, 2008; Manns and Eichenbaum, 2009; Howard and Eichenbaum, 2014), entorhinal (Hafting et al., 2005; Sargolini et al., 2006; Doeller et al., 2010; Chadwick et al., 2015), parahippocampal (PHC; Janzen and van Turennout, 2004; Kravitz et al., 2011; Mullally and Maguire, 2011; Epstein and Vass, 2014), retrosplenial (RSC; Chen et al., 1994; Cho and Sharp, 2001; Vann et al., 2009; Auger et al., 2012; Auger and Maguire, 2013) and posterior parietal (DiMattia and Kesner, 1988; Husain and Nachev, 2007) cortices have been implicated in representing space and facilitating navigation therein, with generally concordant findings across species.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research studies across different species.

claim: Entorhinal cortex has been implicated in representing space and facilitating navigation.
source: Numerous brain areas, including the hippocampus (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Rosenbaum et al., 2004; Spiers and Maguire, 2006; Bird and Burgess, 2008; Manns and Eichenbaum, 2009; Howard and Eichenbaum, 2014), entorhinal (Hafting et al., 2005; Sargolini et al., 2006; Doeller et al., 2010; Chadwick et al., 2015), parahippocampal (PHC; Janzen and van Turennout, 2004; Kravitz et al., 2011; Mullally and Maguire, 2011; Epstein and Vass, 2014), retrosplenial (RSC; Chen et al., 1994; Cho and Sharp, 2001; Vann et al., 2009; Auger et al., 2012; Auger and Maguire, 2013) and posterior parietal (DiMattia and Kesner, 1988; Husain and Nachev, 2007) cortices have been implicated in representing space and facilitating navigation therein, with generally concordant findings across species.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on entorhinal cortex.

claim: Parahippocampal cortex (PHC) has been implicated in representing space and facilitating navigation.
source: Numerous brain areas, including the hippocampus (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Rosenbaum et al., 2004; Spiers and Maguire, 2006; Bird and Burgess, 2008; Manns and Eichenbaum, 2009; Howard and Eichenbaum, 2014), entorhinal (Hafting et al., 2005; Sargolini et al., 2006; Doeller et al., 2010; Chadwick et al., 2015), parahippocampal (PHC; Janzen and van Turennout, 2004; Kravitz et al., 2011; Mullally and Maguire, 2011; Epstein and Vass, 2014), retrosplenial (RSC; Chen et al., 1994; Cho and Sharp, 2001; Vann et al., 2009; Auger et al., 2012; Auger and Maguire, 2013) and posterior parietal (DiMattia and Kesner, 1988; Husain and Nachev, 2007) cortices have been implicated in representing space and facilitating navigation therein, with generally concordant findings across species.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on parahippocampal cortex.

claim: Retrosplenial cortex (RSC) has been implicated in representing space and facilitating navigation.
source: Numerous brain areas, including the hippocampus (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Rosenbaum et al., 2004; Spiers and Maguire, 2006; Bird and Burgess, 2008; Manns and Eichenbaum, 2009; Howard and Eichenbaum, 2014), entorhinal (Hafting et al., 2005; Sargolini et al., 2006; Doeller et al., 2010; Chadwick et al., 2015), parahippocampal (PHC; Janzen and van Turennout, 2004; Kravitz et al., 2011; Mullally and Maguire, 2011; Epstein and Vass, 2014), retrosplenial (RSC; Chen et al., 1994; Cho and Sharp, 2001; Vann et al., 2009; Auger et al., 2012; Auger and Maguire, 2013) and posterior parietal (DiMattia and Kesner, 1988; Husain and Nachev, 2007) cortices have been implicated in representing space and facilitating navigation therein, with generally concordant findings across species.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on retrosplenial cortex.

claim: Posterior parietal cortex has been implicated in representing space and facilitating navigation.
source: Numerous brain areas, including the hippocampus (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Rosenbaum et al., 2004; Spiers and Maguire, 2006; Bird and Burgess, 2008; Manns and Eichenbaum, 2009; Howard and Eichenbaum, 2014), entorhinal (Hafting et al., 2005; Sargolini et al., 2006; Doeller et al., 2010; Chadwick et al., 2015), parahippocampal (PHC; Janzen and van Turennout, 2004; Kravitz et al., 2011; Mullally and Maguire, 2011; Epstein and Vass, 2014), retrosplenial (RSC; Chen et al., 1994; Cho and Sharp, 2001; Vann et al., 2009; Auger et al., 2012; Auger and Maguire, 2013) and posterior parietal (DiMattia and Kesner, 1988; Husain and Nachev, 2007) cortices have been implicated in representing space and facilitating navigation therein, with generally concordant findings across species.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on posterior parietal cortex.

claim: There is a gap in knowledge about how an environmental representation evolves de novo and the roles played by space-sensitive brain regions in this process.
source: We still lack, however, a precise account of how an environmental representation evolves de novo and the roles played by space-sensitive brain regions in this process.
evidence: The authors state this as a gap in the literature based on their review of existing research.

claim: Recent research has studied how neuronal responses in the medial temporal lobes develop in rodent pups when they interact with the world for the first time.
source: In recent years, there has been a move to study how neuronal responses in the medial temporal lobes develop in rodent pups when they interact with the world for the first time (Langston et al., 2010; Wills et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on rodent pups.

claim: In the majority of VR scanning experiments, subjects become familiarised with an environment before scanning and then perform tasks during scanning based on the environmental representation they formed pre-scan.
source: In the majority of these experiments subjects become familiarised with an environment before scanning and then typically perform tasks during scanning based on the environmental representation they formed pre-scan (e.g., Janzen and van Turennout, 2004; Spiers and Maguire, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior VR scanning studies.

claim: A smaller number of VR scanning studies have focused on the acquisition phase of environmental knowledge.
source: A smaller number of VR scanning studies have focused on the acquisition phase of environmental knowledge (e.g., Wolbers et al., 2004; Wolbers and Buchel, 2005; Iaria et al., 2007; Baumann et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior VR studies focused on acquisition.

claim: In every prior VR scanning study, the environments contained landmarks and structures that were readily recognisable and nameable.
source: However, as far as we are aware, in every case the environments contained landmarks and structures that were readily recognisable and nameable (e.g., shops and houses).
evidence: The authors state this based on their review of the literature.

claim: The neural substrates of learning about an environment from scratch, with no prior experience of key elements within it, has never been examined in humans.
source: Thus, the neural substrates of learning about an environment from scratch, with no prior experience of, or knowledge about, key elements within it, has never been examined in humans.
evidence: The authors state this as a gap in the literature based on their review.

claim: Prominent features in an environment, namely landmarks, have been posited to play a fundamental role in how children and adult humans learn about new environments.
source: Prominent features in an environment, namely landmarks, have been posited to play a fundamental role (Tolman, 1948; Lynch, 1960; Siegel and White, 1975; Downs and Stea, 1977; Golledge, 1991; Lew, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Encoding landmarks facilitates the development of route knowledge, and learning how routes relate to each other provides the navigator with a 'survey' representation of an environment.
source: It has been further suggested that encoding landmarks facilitates the development of route knowledge, and learning how routes relate to each other then provides the navigator with a 'survey' representation of an environment (Siegel and White, 1975; Epstein and Vass, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: PHC responded to visuospatial features of landmarks.
source: Auger et al. (2012); (see also Mullally and Maguire, 2011; Konkle and Oliva, 2012; Auger and Maguire, 2013) using fMRI found that PHC responded to visuospatial features of landmarks.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies.

claim: RSC was engaged only when subjects viewed landmarks that had a permanent location and never moved.
source: By contrast RSC was engaged only when subjects viewed landmarks that had a permanent location and never moved (a finding that has since been replicated—Marchette et al., 2014; Troiani et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies.

claim: A function of the RSC may be to code for permanent landmarks on which a stable spatial representation of an environment can then be built.
source: This suggests that a function of the RSC may be to code for permanent landmarks on which a stable spatial representation of an environment can then be built.
evidence: The authors propose this interpretation based on prior findings about RSC responses to permanent landmarks.

claim: The landmarks examined in previous studies were of a type already familiar to subjects.
source: But, as with the work mentioned above, the landmarks examined in these studies were of a type already familiar to subjects.
evidence: The authors state this based on their review of prior studies.

claim: The permanent and transient landmark groups were matched in terms of visual salience, how well they could be remembered, and other features.
source: The landmarks were developed and characterised in an initial experiment with separate subjects (detailed in the 'Materials and methods') ensuring that the permanent and transient landmark groups were matched in terms of visual salience, how well they could be remembered, as well as other features.
evidence: The authors describe their experimental design and landmark characterization procedure.

claim: Subjects were instructed to learn the layout of the environment and told that they would be tested in a variety of ways after scanning.
source: Before scanning, subjects were instructed to learn the layout of the environment and told that they would be tested in a variety of ways after scanning without the specific nature of those tasks being revealed.
evidence: The authors describe the instructions given to participants.

claim: Subjects were informed that some of the landmarks would always remain in the same location whereas others would appear in a different place every time they saw them.
source: They were informed that some of the landmarks would always remain in the same location whereas others would appear in a different place every time they saw them.
evidence: The authors describe the instructions given to participants.

claim: The world contained five different coloured intersecting straight paths.
source: The world contained five different coloured intersecting straight paths (yellow, red, grey, blue and green; Figure 1C).
evidence: The authors describe the environment design and reference Figure 1C.

claim: Each path had 12 landmarks (six permanent, six transient) evenly distributed alongside it.
source: Each path had 12 landmarks (six permanent, six transient) evenly distributed alongside it (Figure 1B).
evidence: The authors describe the environment design and reference Figure 1B.

claim: The environment was covered in a shroud of fog to restrict the field of view and ensure complete control over the exposure subjects had to each landmark.
source: In these videos, the environment was covered in a shroud of fog to restrict the field of view thus ensuring we had complete control over the exposure subjects had to each landmark (Figure 2A)—hence we refer to the environment as 'Fog World' (see Video 1).
evidence: The authors describe their experimental design and reference Figure 2A and Video 1.

claim: There was no difference in the rate at which subjects learned to recognise permanent and transient landmarks.
source: We then directly compared the slopes and found that there was no difference in the rate at which subjects learned to recognise permanent and transient landmarks (mean difference in rate = 0.0084, SD = 0.063; t31 = 0.763, p = 0.45).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: There was a significant time by landmark type interaction in recognition accuracy across the four learning quarters.
source: We then examined recognition accuracy in each of the four learning quarters and observed a significant time (quarters) by landmark type (permanent, transient) interaction (F3,29 = 8.045, p = 0.0005).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Participants recognised permanent and transient landmarks equally in the first quarter.
source: Interrogating this result further, we found that that participants recognised permanent and transient landmarks equally in the first quarter (mean accuracy permanent landmarks = 57.7% (SD 9.7); transient landmarks = 58.1% (SD 17.7); t31 = 0.12, p = 0.9)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Participants recognised permanent and transient landmarks equally in the final quarter.
source: and final quarter (permanent landmarks = 79.6% (SD 18.3); transient landmarks = 77.3% (SD 14); t31 = 0.55, p = 0.6).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: In the second quarter, participants were more accurate in their recognition of permanent than transient landmarks.
source: In the second quarter (permanent landmarks = 72.7% (SD 14.4); transient landmarks = 60.4% (SD 13.1); t31 = 3.517, p = 0.001)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: In the third quarter, participants were more accurate in their recognition of permanent than transient landmarks.
source: and third quarter (permanent landmarks = 80.0% (SD 15.6); transient landmarks = 70.4% (SD 16.3); t31 = 2.361, p = 0.02), however, participants were more accurate in their recognition of permanent than transient landmarks.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: In the post-scan testing phase, there was no difference in how well subjects recognised permanent or transient landmarks.
source: Consistent with the result in the final quarter of learning, in the post-scan testing phase, there was no difference in how well subjects recognised permanent or transient landmarks ('memorableness': permanent mean accuracy = 82.9% (SD 4.9); transient mean accuracy = 76.3% (SD 4.4); t31 = 1.745, p = 0.09).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Subjects were accurate at identifying as novel landmarks which they had not seen before.
source: Subjects were also accurate at identifying as novel landmarks which they had not seen before (mean = 93.0%, SD 2.3).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data.

claim: Permanence ratings made post-fMRI scan were strongly correlated with the actual values.
source: Permanence ratings made post-fMRI scan were strongly correlated with the actual values (r = 0.793, p < 0.0001), indicating that subjects had successfully learned this information.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Size ratings in the post-scan session were significantly correlated with the actual landmarks sizes in Fog World.
source: Similarly, the size ratings in the post-scan session were significantly correlated with the actual landmarks sizes in Fog World (r = 0.726, p < 0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The visual salience of landmarks was influenced by how and where they had been experienced within the environment.
source: In other words, the visual salience of landmarks (or how 'attention grabbing' they were) was not just an inherent property; it was also influenced by how and where they had been experienced within the environment.
evidence: The authors infer this from the correlation patterns between salience ratings and landmark properties.

claim: The factor analysis confirmed the presence of four independent components in the landmark features, which included permanence of landmarks as a distinct factor.
source: Thus the factor analysis confirmed the presence of four independent components in the landmark features, which included permanence of landmarks as a distinct factor.
evidence: The claim is supported by the results of the principal components factor analysis.

claim: There was a good deal of variance in navigation task performance.
source: As we expected and hoped, there was a good deal of variance in navigation task performance (mean score = 12.8, SD = 8.1).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from the navigation task.

claim: Participants were not merely making simple path colour to landmark associations in the navigation task.
source: This suggests that participants were not merely making simple path colour to landmark associations, and in fact identifying the part and side of path was where more marks were scored (part vs path: t31 = −2.121, p = 0.042).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of navigation task performance.

claim: Only two out of thirty two participants made reference to specifically focussing on the permanence of the landmarks.
source: Only two out of thirty two participants made reference to specifically focussing on the permanence of the landmarks.
evidence: The claim is supported by post-scan debriefing data.

claim: There were numerous large clusters of increased activity more for permanent than transient landmarks across the whole scanning experiment.
source: We first examined the fMRI data by directly comparing permanent with transient landmarks across the whole scanning experiment. There were numerous large clusters of increased activity more for permanent than transient landmarks: one including left RSC and PHC (−21, −49, −8, z = 6.01; −12, −43, 1, z = 5.72), another including right RSC and PHC (9, −52, 4, z = 5.10; 30, −49, −5, z = 5.14), and others in left occipital cortex (−15, −88, 25, z = 5.78; −9, −85, 4, z = 4.95), left and right superior posterior parieto-occipital sulcus (POS; −3, −76, 40, z = 5.24; 15, −61, 19, z = 4.94) as well as left lateral temporal cortex (−51, −43, 4, z = 5.61), right occipital cortex (18, −88, 22, z = 5.50; 27, −82, 31) and posterior parietal cortex/precuneus (0, −34, 46, z = 4.89).
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data analysis.

claim: No regions were more active for transient than permanent landmarks.
source: No regions were more active for transient than permanent landmarks.
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data analysis.

claim: By the final quarter of learning there were significantly greater responses to the permanent landmarks compared to the transient in right and left RSC.
source: By the final quarter of learning (the last three learning sweeps) there were significantly greater responses to the permanent landmarks compared to the transient in right (6, −53, 5; Z = 5.41) and left (−6, −55, 10; Z = 5.90) RSC, as well as right POS (9, −73, 31; Z = 5.01) and posteriorly in the left occipital lobe (−6, −79, −8; Z = 5.00) (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 4.

claim: There were activations in the hippocampus and PHC for permanent vs transient landmarks in the final quarter at a reduced threshold.
source: There were also activations in the hippocampus (−21, −28, −11; Z = 3.71) and PHC (21, −37, −14; Z = 4.12) but at a reduced threshold (p < 0.0001 uncorrected; compared with the whole-brain FWE corrected p < 0.05 reported otherwise).
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data analysis at a specified threshold.

claim: The increased responses to permanent landmarks were present as early as the third quarter of scanning in similar regions including RSC.
source: The increased responses to permanent landmarks were even present as early as the third quarter of scanning (sweeps 7–9 of 12) in similar regions (right RSC: 12, −51, 3; Z = 5.31; left RSC: −12, −55, 6; Z = 5.72; left POS: −6, −76, 40; Z = 4.93; left occipital: −15, −76, −11; Z = 5.53), but not in the hippocampus or PHC.
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data analysis.

claim: There were no differences between responses to permanent and transient landmarks in either of the first two quarters of learning.
source: There were no differences between responses to permanent and transient landmarks in either of the first two quarters of learning.
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data analysis.

claim: Increasing values of the permanence-related factor were associated with activations in left lateral temporal cortex, left occipital cortex, left PHC, left RSC, right RSC and posterior parietal cortex/precuneus across the entire scanning session.
source: Considering first the permanence-related factor (factor 1), namely fMRI responses associated with increasing values of this factor across the entire scanning session, the results were in line with the categorical contrast reported above: left lateral temporal cortex (−60, −40, 1; z = 6.14), left occipital cortex (−15, −91, 25, z = 5.86; −9, −64, −2, z = 4.94; −15, −73, −8, z = 4.86; −12, −31, −5, z = 4.66; −9, −85, 4, z = 4.64), left PHC (−21, −49, −5, z = 5.29), left RSC (−9, −43, 1, z = 5.03; −9, −52, 10, z = 4.61), right RSC (9, −49, 4, z = 4.90) and posterior parietal cortex/precuneus (0, −58, 43, z = 5.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data analysis using parametric regressors.

claim: No areas showed responses associated with decreasing values of the permanence factor.
source: No areas showed responses associated with decreasing values of this permanence factor.
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data analysis.

claim: Increasing values of the permanence-related factor were associated with significant activations in bilateral RSC and POS in the final quarter of learning.
source: Increasing values of the permanence-related factor were associated with significant activations in bilateral RSC (left: −12, −55, 7; Z = 5.60; right: 9, −52, 4; Z = 5.12), as well as POS (left: −9, −91, 25; Z = 5.59; right: 9, −73, 31; Z = 5.54) in the final quarter of learning, but only right RSC in the third quarter (12, −48, 1; Z = 5.03) and no regions in either of the first 2 quarters (top of Figure 3B, in blue).
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There were increased responses in the left hippocampus and right PHC at a reduced threshold in the last quarter of scanning for the permanence factor.
source: Once again there were also increased responses in the left hippocampus (−18, −28, −11; Z = 3.99) and right PHC (24, −37, −14; Z = 4.24) but at a reduced threshold (p < 0.0001 uncorrected) in the last quarter of scanning.
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data analysis at a specified threshold.

claim: Better remembered landmarks were associated with increased activations in left occipital, left postero-lateral parietal, and left temporal cortices, as well as bilateral POS and bilateral RSC.
source: We then considered factor 2, the 'memorableness' factor, namely those landmarks that were better remembered, and again began by examining fMRI responses associated with increasing values of this factor across the entire scanning session. The better remembered landmarks were associated with increased activations in left occipital (−9, −79, −8, Z = 6.54), left postero-lateral parietal (−48, −52, 34, Z = 6.29), and left temporal (−63, −37, −2, Z = 5.81) cortices, as well as bilateral POS (left: −6, −67, 34, Z = 5.87; right: 6, −64, 43, Z = 5.62) and bilateral RSC (left: −6, −49, 7, Z = 5.10; right: 6, −52, 13, Z = 4.69).
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data analysis using parametric regressors.

claim: The more easily remembered landmarks did not produce any significant activation in the final quarter of learning.
source: Investigating the source of these changes showed that the more easily remembered landmarks (those with greater values for factor 2) did not produce any significant activation in the final quarter of learning.
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data analysis.

claim: At the start of learning (in the first quarter), there was a greater response in POS to landmarks which participants went on to later remember better in both the right and left hemispheres.
source: However, at the start of learning (in the first quarter), there was a greater response in POS to landmarks which participants went on to later remember better in both the right (15, −70, 31; Z = 5.35) and left (−9, −76, 28; Z = 5.30) hemispheres (second row of Figure 3B, in red).
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The POS initially responded to memorable landmarks but then switched its response to permanent ones.
source: Thus, the POS initially responded to memorable landmarks but then switched its response to permanent ones (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Responses to the size and visual salience related factors remained constant throughout learning, with the greatest activations consistently occurring in posterior, visual areas.
source: Responses to the size and visual salience related factors (factors 3 and 4 respectively) remained constant throughout learning, with the greatest activations (associated with increased values on these factors) consistently occurring in posterior, visual areas (Figure 3B in green and purple respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: As subjects learned the permanence of landmarks, a representation emerged within the RSC.
source: In summary, as subjects learned the permanence of landmarks, a representation emerged within the RSC (factor 1).
evidence: The authors summarize their fMRI findings.

claim: POS developed responses to permanent landmarks, but this region was also initially activated by landmarks which were subsequently better remembered.
source: POS also developed responses to permanent landmarks, but this region was also initially activated by landmarks which were subsequently better remembered (factor 2).
evidence: The authors summarize their fMRI findings.

claim: The hippocampus and PHC were eventually more engaged by the most stable items, but later on and less strongly than RSC and POS.
source: The hippocampus and PHC were eventually more engaged by the most stable items, but later on and less strongly than RSC and POS.
evidence: The authors summarize their fMRI findings.

claim: Perceptual features of the landmarks, their visual salience and size, were associated with tonic responses throughout learning in posterior visual areas.
source: Perceptual features of the landmarks, their visual salience and size, were associated with tonic responses throughout learning in posterior visual areas (factors 3 and 4).
evidence: The authors summarize their fMRI findings.

claim: As subjects learned to distinguish permanent from transient landmarks, responses within their RSC directly reflected their knowledge of this difference.
source: Therefore as subjects learned to distinguish permanent from transient landmarks, responses within their RSC directly reflected their knowledge of this difference.
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI analysis using subject-specific learning models.

claim: The greatest activation related to subject-specific permanence learning was in the RSC.
source: The greatest activation was in the RSC (9, −58, 22; Z = 4.38), a second peak was also present in the body of the caudate nucleus (18, −10, 25; Z = 4.03).
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI analysis using subject-specific learning models.

claim: In the second half of learning both RSC and POS showed increased functional coupling with the hippocampus when viewing permanent compared to transient landmarks.
source: In the second half of learning both regions showed increased functional coupling with the hippocampus when viewing permanent compared to transient landmarks. For both RSC (right RSC: 21, −16, −23; Z = 4.23; left RSC: −30, −10, −26; Z = 3.42) and POS (right POS: 30, −7, 20; Z = 3.70; left POS: −30, −13, −20; Z = 3.89), this greater functional connectivity was with anterior parts of the hippocampus bilaterally.
evidence: The claim is supported by PPI connectivity analysis.

claim: Neither RSC nor POS showed any differences in connectivity related to permanence during the first half of learning.
source: Neither RSC nor POS showed any differences in connectivity related to permanence during the first half of learning; these only emerged as subjects learned the stability of landmarks.
evidence: The claim is supported by PPI connectivity analysis.

claim: As subjects learned the permanence of landmarks, RSC increased its functional connectivity with the hippocampus.
source: Using the same parts of RSC where greater responses emerged as subjects learned the permanence of landmarks as a seed region (Figure 6), the greatest increase in functional coupling developed with the left hippocampus (−30, −28, −14; Z = 3.99). Thus, as subjects learned the permanence of landmarks, their RSC not only developed greater responses to the permanent landmarks but also increased its functional connectivity with the hippocampus.
evidence: The claim is supported by PPI connectivity analysis using subject-specific learning models and shown in Figure 6.

claim: RSC, POS and PHC did not have any activity related to knowledge of permanent landmark locations at any point throughout the scanning experiment.
source: RSC, POS and PHC did not have any activity related to knowledge of permanent landmark locations at any point throughout the scanning experiment (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by MVB analysis and shown in Figure 7.

claim: There were no significant results for the hippocampus during the first three quarters of learning in the MVB analysis.
source: Similarly, there were no significant results for the hippocampus during the first three quarters of learning.
evidence: The claim is supported by MVB analysis.

claim: In the final quarter of the learning period, hippocampal responses emerged which were significantly related to the amount of information about the locations of permanent landmarks.
source: However, in the final quarter of the learning period, hippocampal responses emerged which were significantly related to the amount of information about the locations of permanent landmarks (log model evidence = 12.8; posterior probability = 1.0).
evidence: The claim is supported by MVB analysis.

claim: In contrast to the RSC which responded to accruing knowledge of landmark permanence per se, by the end of the learning phase, activity patterns within the hippocampus mapped onto how much subjects knew about where those permanent landmarks were located within Fog World.
source: In summary, in contrast to the RSC which responded to accruing knowledge of landmark permanence per se, by the end of the learning phase, activity patterns within the hippocampus mapped onto how much subjects knew about where those permanent landmarks were located within Fog World.
evidence: The authors summarize their MVB findings.

claim: RSC played a central and highly selective role by representing only the most stable, permanent features in Fog World.
source: Retrosplenial cortex (RSC) played a central and highly selective role by representing only the most stable, permanent features in this world.
evidence: The authors state this as a main finding in the abstract.

claim: Subsequently, increased coupling was noted between RSC and hippocampus, with hippocampus then expressing knowledge of permanent landmark locations and overall environmental layout.
source: Subsequently, increased coupling was noted between RSC and hippocampus, with hippocampus then expressing knowledge of permanent landmark locations and overall environmental layout.
evidence: The authors state this as a main finding in the abstract.

claim: RSC became selectively engaged by non-moving, permanent landmarks and not those which constantly changed their location as the 'alien' landmarks were learned.
source: We found that as the 'alien' landmarks were learned, RSC became selectively engaged by non-moving, permanent landmarks and not those which constantly changed their location.
evidence: The authors state this as a main finding in the discussion.

claim: Modelling how much individual subjects knew about the permanence of landmarks throughout the course of learning revealed that this was directly related to activity in RSC.
source: Furthermore, modelling how much individual subjects knew about the permanence of landmarks throughout the course of learning revealed that this was directly related to activity in RSC.
evidence: The authors state this as a main finding in the discussion.

claim: RSC did not take the whole scanning session to develop robust and selective sensitivity to the stable landmarks.
source: It did not even take the whole scanning session for RSC to develop robust and selective sensitivity to the stable landmarks.
evidence: The authors infer this from the timing of RSC activation during learning.

claim: The remarkable adaptability of the RSC permanence representation process hints at it being fundamental for learning about and orientating within our surroundings.
source: This demonstrates the remarkable adaptability of the process and hints at it being fundamental for learning about and orientating within our surroundings.
evidence: The authors speculate about the implications of their findings.

claim: RSC responds to landmark permanence for everyday outdoor items when people are engaged in a completely incidental task.
source: Additionally, in previous work (Auger et al., 2012; Auger and Maguire, 2013), we have demonstrated that RSC responds to landmark permanence (for everyday outdoor items) when people are engaged in a completely incidental task.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: At the start of the learning process, RSC was not responsive to any feature of landmarks.
source: At the start of the learning process, RSC was not responsive to any feature of landmarks.
evidence: The authors state this based on their fMRI findings.

claim: It was only during the third quarter of scanning that RSC became engaged at all, specifically reacting to permanent landmarks.
source: Indeed, it was only during the third quarter of scanning that RSC became engaged at all, specifically reacting to permanent landmarks.
evidence: The authors state this based on their fMRI findings.

claim: The representation that develops in RSC is not only very sensitive to permanence but it is also highly specific.
source: This is an important distinction as it indicates that the representation that develops in RSC is not only very sensitive to permanence but it is also highly specific.
evidence: The authors infer this from the comparison of RSC and POS response profiles.

claim: In the absence of reliable information regarding the permanence of landmarks, RSC did not just respond to some other feature.
source: In the absence of reliable information regarding the permanence of landmarks, RSC did not just respond to some other feature.
evidence: The authors state this based on their fMRI findings.

claim: RSC and POS are cytoarchitecturally distinct and have different connectivity.
source: However, RSC and POS are cytoarchitecturally distinct and have different connectivity (Vann et al., 2009), and given that we have now pinpointed differences in their responsivity, we suggest caution in using the over-general term retrosplenial complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior anatomical work.

claim: Activity in the RSC was directly related to how well people knew the permanence of items.
source: Activity in the RSC was directly related to how well people knew the permanence of items.
evidence: The authors state this based on their fMRI analysis using subject-specific learning models.

claim: The permanence representation in RSC is not just a simple binary response which indicates whether or not an item is known to be stable.
source: This reveals that the permanence representation that emerges is not just a simple binary response which indicates whether or not an item is known to be stable.
evidence: The authors infer this from the relationship between RSC activity and learning state.

claim: The RSC permanence representation appears to be more informative, relating to the precision with which the permanence of landmarks is known.
source: Instead it appears to be more informative, relating to the precision with which the permanence of landmarks is known.
evidence: The authors infer this from the relationship between RSC activity and learning state.

claim: In addition to identifying the most stable environmental cues, the RSC could also indicate how reliable subsequent representations based upon such cues might be.
source: In addition, therefore, to identifying the most stable environmental cues, the RSC could also indicate how reliable subsequent representations based upon such cues might be.
evidence: The authors speculate about the functional implications of their findings.

claim: POS was not implicated in processing permanent landmarks in previous experiments.
source: This region was not implicated in processing permanent landmarks in previous experiments (e.g., Auger et al., 2012; Auger and Maguire, 2013).
evidence: The authors state this based on their review of prior work.

claim: POS may be tuned to navigationally 'useful' landmarks.
source: For example, it could be that POS is tuned to navigationally 'useful' landmarks.
evidence: The authors speculate about the function of POS based on their findings.

claim: POS may play a role in relating landmarks with a specific location.
source: Alternatively, our results could indicate POS plays a role in relating landmarks with a specific location.
evidence: The authors speculate about the function of POS based on their findings.

claim: While RSC appears specialised in processing the permanence of landmarks, the response profile of POS is more consistent with it playing some role in indexing navigational utility, or perhaps relating landmarks with the discrete locations where they have been encountered.
source: Therefore, while RSC appears specialised in processing the permanence of landmarks, the response profile of POS is more consistent with it playing some role in indexing navigational utility, or perhaps relating landmarks with the discrete locations where they have been encountered.
evidence: The authors interpret their findings about POS function.

claim: Unlike RSC, activity in the hippocampus was not directly related to how well subjects had learned the permanence of landmarks.
source: Furthermore, unlike RSC, activity in the hippocampus was not directly related to how well subjects had learned the permanence of landmarks.
evidence: The authors state this based on their fMRI findings.

claim: Whereas RSC tracked the acquisition of permanence knowledge, the hippocampus was only engaged by landmarks which were both known to be permanent and associated with a specific place.
source: Whereas RSC tracked the acquisition of permanence knowledge, the hippocampus was only engaged by landmarks which were both known to be permanent and associated with a specific place.
evidence: The authors interpret their findings about hippocampal function.

claim: Once the hippocampal representation had emerged, it contained spatial detail related to how much subjects knew about where the permanent landmarks were located.
source: The MVB analysis indicated that once the hippocampal representation had emerged, it contained spatial detail related to how much subjects knew about where the permanent landmarks were located.
evidence: The authors state this based on their MVB analysis.

claim: The landmark-location representations in POS may have been discrete and local to a particular landmark, while the spatial detail decoded in the hippocampus was related to the wider knowledge of the environment's overall layout and the location of all the permanent landmarks within it.
source: Moreover, the landmark-location representations in POS may have been discrete and local to a particular landmark, while the spatial detail decoded in the hippocampus was related to the wider knowledge of the environment's overall layout and the location of all the permanent landmarks within it.
evidence: The authors speculate about the differences between POS and hippocampal representations.

claim: The RSC may code for the stability of features within an environment, potentially providing this as an input to the hippocampus, which could in turn utilise the information to build detailed spatial representations based upon the most reliable cues.
source: It seems then that the RSC may code for the stability of features within an environment, potentially providing this as an input to the hippocampus, which could in turn utilise the information to build detailed spatial representations based upon the most reliable cues.
evidence: The authors propose this model based on their findings about RSC-hippocampal connectivity and function.

claim: In the macaque monkey, RSC sends extensive cortical efferent projections to the medial temporal lobes.
source: In the macaque monkey, RSC sends extensive cortical efferent projections to the medial temporal lobes (presubiculum, parasubiculum, entorhinal and PHC cortex; Kobayashi and Amaral, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to anatomical tracer studies.

claim: RSC receives inputs from similar regions, most notably the hippocampal formation, PHC and perirhinal cortices.
source: It receives inputs from similar regions, most notably the hippocampal formation (entorhinal cortex, subiculum, presubiculum and parasubiculum), PHC and perirhinal cortices.
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical knowledge.

claim: Area 29 receives a large majority of projections from the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex.
source: In particular, Area 29 receives a large majority of projections from the hippocampus (both subiculum and presubiculum) and entorhinal cortex (Aggleton et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to anatomical studies.

claim: Many studies have reported RSC and anterior hippocampus co-activating in fMRI studies.
source: This is also in keeping with many studies that have reported RSC and anterior hippocampus co-activing in fMRI studies (e.g., Zeidman et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior fMRI studies.

claim: Inactivation of RSC in rats is associated with disruption of hippocampal place fields.
source: In addition, inactivation of RSC in rats is associated with disruption of hippocampal place fields (Cooper and Mizumori, 2001), and previous studies have reported hippocampal involvement in retrieving spatial information about objects (Save et al., 1992; Manns and Eichenbaum, 2009; Baumann et al., 2010; Ekstrom et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior animal studies.

claim: Previous studies have reported hippocampal involvement in retrieving spatial information about objects.
source: In addition, inactivation of RSC in rats is associated with disruption of hippocampal place fields (Cooper and Mizumori, 2001), and previous studies have reported hippocampal involvement in retrieving spatial information about objects (Save et al., 1992; Manns and Eichenbaum, 2009; Baumann et al., 2010; Ekstrom et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Object-centred firing has been observed in rodent lateral entorhinal and anterior cingulate cortex.
source: We did not find responses relating to the landmarks in any other brain regions, but object-centred firing has also been observed in rodent lateral entorhinal (Deshmukh and Knierim, 2012) and anterior cingulate cortex (Weible et al., 2012), even for locations formerly (but no longer) occupied by objects (Tsao et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior animal studies.

claim: The present study provides an alternative interpretation of previous work which found that RSC is engaged when making judgements about locations relative to stable items.
source: The present study provides an alternative interpretation of previous work which found that RSC is engaged when making judgements about locations relative to stable items (Committeri et al., 2004; Sulpizio et al., 2013).
evidence: The authors propose a reinterpretation of prior findings based on their results.

claim: Previous studies concluded that activity within the RSC reflected coding of space relative to stable landmarks.
source: These previous studies concluded that activity within the RSC reflected coding of space relative to stable landmarks.
evidence: The authors describe the conclusions of prior studies.

claim: The current findings suggest RSC activity could indicate a more fundamental representation of the landmark itself, specifically that of its inherent permanence.
source: However, our findings suggest it could in fact indicate a more fundamental representation of the landmark itself, specifically that of its inherent permanence.
evidence: The authors propose this interpretation based on their findings.

claim: The elementary discrimination between stable and moving landmarks within RSC is used to anchor representations of surrounding space.
source: We suggest that the elementary discrimination between stable and moving landmarks demonstrated here within RSC is used to anchor representations of surrounding space.
evidence: The authors propose this functional interpretation based on their findings.

claim: Head direction cells have been found in rodent RSC.
source: This could be linked to the presence of head direction cells within the rodent RSC (Chen et al., 1994; Cho and Sharp, 2001), perhaps suggesting that head direction cell firing is centred upon permanent landmarks and this information is integrated within RSC.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior animal studies.

claim: Head direction cells account for approximately 8% of cells in rodent RSC.
source: While head direction cells have been found in rodent RSC (Chen et al., 1994; Cho and Sharp, 2001), it has been estimated that these only account for approximately 8% of cells (Chen et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior animal studies.

claim: The discrimination between permanent and transient landmarks in RSC may go some way towards explaining its strong, ubiquitous engagement during fMRI studies of scene processing.
source: The discrimination between permanent and transient landmarks in RSC could play a crucial role in a number of fundamental computations involving space. It may go some way towards explaining its strong, ubiquitous engagement during fMRI studies of scene processing (Epstein, 2008; Howard et al., 2014; Zeidman et al., 2014), while navigating (Maguire, 2001a; Hartley et al., 2003; Spiers and Maguire, 2006; Spreng et al., 2009; Vann et al., 2009), recalling autobiographical memories (Maguire, 2001b; Gardini et al., 2006; Steinvorth et al., 2006; Svoboda et al., 2006; Cabeza and St Jacques, 2007; Spreng et al., 2009) and imagining future and fictitious events (Addis et al., 2007; Hassabis et al., 2007; Szpunar et al., 2007; Botzung et al., 2008; Summerfield et al., 2009).
evidence: The authors speculate about the broader implications of their findings, supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: RSC is strongly and ubiquitously engaged during fMRI studies of navigation.
source: The discrimination between permanent and transient landmarks in RSC could play a crucial role in a number of fundamental computations involving space. It may go some way towards explaining its strong, ubiquitous engagement during fMRI studies of scene processing (Epstein, 2008; Howard et al., 2014; Zeidman et al., 2014), while navigating (Maguire, 2001a; Hartley et al., 2003; Spiers and Maguire, 2006; Spreng et al., 2009; Vann et al., 2009), recalling autobiographical memories (Maguire, 2001b; Gardini et al., 2006; Steinvorth et al., 2006; Svoboda et al., 2006; Cabeza and St Jacques, 2007; Spreng et al., 2009) and imagining future and fictitious events (Addis et al., 2007; Hassabis et al., 2007; Szpunar et al., 2007; Botzung et al., 2008; Summerfield et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies.

claim: RSC is strongly and ubiquitously engaged during fMRI studies of recalling autobiographical memories.
source: The discrimination between permanent and transient landmarks in RSC could play a crucial role in a number of fundamental computations involving space. It may go some way towards explaining its strong, ubiquitous engagement during fMRI studies of scene processing (Epstein, 2008; Howard et al., 2014; Zeidman et al., 2014), while navigating (Maguire, 2001a; Hartley et al., 2003; Spiers and Maguire, 2006; Spreng et al., 2009; Vann et al., 2009), recalling autobiographical memories (Maguire, 2001b; Gardini et al., 2006; Steinvorth et al., 2006; Svoboda et al., 2006; Cabeza and St Jacques, 2007; Spreng et al., 2009) and imagining future and fictitious events (Addis et al., 2007; Hassabis et al., 2007; Szpunar et al., 2007; Botzung et al., 2008; Summerfield et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies.

claim: RSC is strongly and ubiquitously engaged during fMRI studies of imagining future and fictitious events.
source: The discrimination between permanent and transient landmarks in RSC could play a crucial role in a number of fundamental computations involving space. It may go some way towards explaining its strong, ubiquitous engagement during fMRI studies of scene processing (Epstein, 2008; Howard et al., 2014; Zeidman et al., 2014), while navigating (Maguire, 2001a; Hartley et al., 2003; Spiers and Maguire, 2006; Spreng et al., 2009; Vann et al., 2009), recalling autobiographical memories (Maguire, 2001b; Gardini et al., 2006; Steinvorth et al., 2006; Svoboda et al., 2006; Cabeza and St Jacques, 2007; Spreng et al., 2009) and imagining future and fictitious events (Addis et al., 2007; Hassabis et al., 2007; Szpunar et al., 2007; Botzung et al., 2008; Summerfield et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies.

claim: All of scene processing, navigation, autobiographical memory, and imagining future events involve picturing scenes or events, with RSC possibly signalling the presence of permanent features.
source: All of these involve picturing scenes or events, with RSC possibly signalling the presence of permanent features (Auger and Maguire, 2013).
evidence: The authors propose this interpretation based on their findings and prior work.

claim: Otherwise healthy individuals who were poor navigators had difficulty reliably identifying permanent landmarks.
source: Auger et al. (2012) and Auger and Maguire (2013) found that otherwise healthy individuals who were poor navigators had difficulty reliably identifying permanent landmarks, and had reduced responses in RSC compared to good navigators when viewing permanent landmarks.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Poor navigators had reduced responses in RSC compared to good navigators when viewing permanent landmarks.
source: Auger et al. (2012) and Auger and Maguire (2013) found that otherwise healthy individuals who were poor navigators had difficulty reliably identifying permanent landmarks, and had reduced responses in RSC compared to good navigators when viewing permanent landmarks.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Damage involving the RSC leaves patients unable to derive orientation information from landmarks which they can otherwise recognise.
source: In neuropsychological studies, damage involving the RSC is never focal, but nevertheless leaves patients unable to derive orientation information from landmarks which they can otherwise recognise (Maguire, 2001a; Vann et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior neuropsychological studies.

claim: Metabolic and structural changes in Alzheimer's Disease/Mild Cognitive Impairment have been found to be first centred upon RSC.
source: Metabolic and structural changes in Alzheimer's Disease/Mild Cognitive Impairment have been found to be first centred upon RSC (Villain et al., 2008; Pengas et al., 2010, 2012; Tu et al., 2015), and spatial disorientation is often one of the first signs of the disease.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: Spatial disorientation is often one of the first signs of Alzheimer's Disease.
source: Metabolic and structural changes in Alzheimer's Disease/Mild Cognitive Impairment have been found to be first centred upon RSC (Villain et al., 2008; Pengas et al., 2010, 2012; Tu et al., 2015), and spatial disorientation is often one of the first signs of the disease.
evidence: The claim is based on clinical knowledge about Alzheimer's Disease.

claim: If representations of space are founded upon permanence information from RSC, then it needs to be dependable.
source: If representations of space are founded upon permanence information from RSC, as seems to be indicated by our results, then it needs to be dependable.
evidence: The authors propose this logical inference based on their findings.

claim: If RSC permanence information is not dependable, afflicted individuals may be falling at the first hurdle, and one can understand why spatial disorientation then arises.
source: If this is not the case, afflicted individuals may be falling at the first hurdle, so to speak, and one can understand why spatial disorientation then arises, because upstream regions that rely on good quality input cannot perform optimally to build reliable environmental representations.
evidence: The authors speculate about the implications of RSC dysfunction.

claim: The current results provide compelling evidence that the RSC may be fundamentally concerned with coding for permanent landmarks.
source: We believe that the current results provide compelling evidence that the RSC may be fundamentally concerned with coding for permanent landmarks.
evidence: The authors state their interpretation of their findings.

claim: RSC coding for permanent landmarks may account for its involvement in scene processing, navigation, autobiographical memory and future-thinking, providing input for upstream areas such as the hippocampus to then construct models of the world based upon reliable cues.
source: We further propose that this may account for its involvement in scene processing, navigation, autobiographical memory and future-thinking, providing input for upstream areas such as the hippocampus to then construct models of the world based upon reliable cues (Maguire and Mullally, 2013; Zeidman et al., 2014).
evidence: The authors propose this model based on their findings and cite related theoretical work.

claim: Ten subjects took part in a landmark characterisation study.
source: Ten subjects (five female, mean age 28 years, SD 4.8) took part in a landmark characterisation study.
evidence: The authors describe their experimental methods.

claim: None of the landmark characterisation subjects took part in the subsequent fMRI study.
source: None of these subjects took part in the subsequent fMRI study.
evidence: The authors describe their experimental methods.

claim: 134 unique 3D 'alien' items were created to be used as potential landmarks in Fog World.
source: We created 134 unique 3D 'alien' items to be used as potential landmarks in Fog World (examples in Figure 1A).
evidence: The authors describe their experimental methods and reference Figure 1A.

claim: Two groups of 30 landmarks each were selected from the original set of 134 to be used as the permanent and transient landmarks within the VR environment.
source: Using these ratings, we selected two groups of 30 landmarks each (from the original set of 134) to be used as the permanent and transient landmarks within the VR environment.
evidence: The authors describe their experimental methods.

claim: The two landmark groups did not differ in terms of salience, other associations, likeableness, animateness, or memorableness.
source: These object groups were carefully selected to ensure that they did not differ in terms of any of the features rated (t-tests of the two landmark groups: Salience: t58 = 0.669, p = 0.51; Other associations: t58 = 0.000, p = 1.0; Likeableness: t58 = 0.312, p = 0.76; Animateness: t58 = −1.089, p = 0.28; Memorableness: t58 = 0.247, p = 0.81).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of landmark features.

claim: The landmark groups did not differ in actual size or mean spatial frequency.
source: The landmarks groups did not differ on two other factors—the actual size of the items (when in the VR environment: Small/Medium/Large; [t58 = 0.000, p = 1.0] and mean spatial frequency [t58 = −0.562, p = 0.58]).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of landmark features.

claim: 32 different subjects took part in the fMRI study.
source: 32 different subjects (16 female, mean age 23.7 years, SD 2.4) took part in the fMRI study.
evidence: The authors describe their experimental methods.

claim: Fog World was created using the jMonkeyEngine 3.0 beta game engine, Java JDK 1.6 and Blender.
source: Fog World was created using the jMonkeyEngine 3.0 beta game engine (http://jmonkeyengine.org), Java JDK 1.6 (Sun Microsystems, Santa Clara, California) and Blender (Stichting Blender Foundation, Amsterdam).
evidence: The authors describe their experimental methods.

claim: There were 60 trials in total, with the five paths being travelled 12 times each.
source: There were 60 trials in total, with the five paths being travelled 12 times each (i.e., once per learning sweep).
evidence: The authors describe their experimental design.

claim: Permanent landmarks remained in the same location on each trial, whereas transient landmarks appeared in a different location on every exposure.
source: Permanent landmarks remained in the same location on each trial, whereas transient landmarks appeared in a different location on every exposure.
evidence: The authors describe their experimental design.

claim: The permanent and transient landmarks were placed in equivalent locations within the environment.
source: The locations in which all 60 landmarks appeared on each of the 60 trials were meticulously designed so that permanent and transient landmarks were equally distributed either side and along the whole length of each path. This ensured that the permanent and transient landmarks, as well as being matched for their perceptual features (size, visual salience, and other features—see above), were placed in equivalent locations within the environment.
evidence: The authors describe their experimental design to control for confounds.

claim: Each video took a first person perspective travelling along one of the paths.
source: Each video took a first person perspective travelling along one of the paths.
evidence: The authors describe their experimental design.

claim: When a landmark emerged out of the fog, the camera turned to bring the landmark into the centre of the screen, where it was positioned for 2 s.
source: On each trial, the camera travelled along a path in a straight line. When a landmark emerged out of the fog, the camera turned to bring the landmark into the centre of the screen, where it was positioned for 2 s, the camera then panned back to the middle of the path as it continued travelling forwards (Figure 2A from top to bottom; see also Video 1).
evidence: The authors describe their experimental design and reference Figure 2A and Video 1.

claim: The paths were always travelled in the same direction, with the same start and end point each time.
source: The paths were always travelled in the same direction, with the same start and end point each time.
evidence: The authors describe their experimental design.

claim: Each path intersected with two others.
source: To encourage subjects to learn an integrated representation of the whole environment, the paths intersected one another. Each path intersected with two others (Figure 1C).
evidence: The authors describe their experimental design and reference Figure 1C.

claim: These 60 videos were each approximately 1 min in length.
source: These 60 videos (corresponding to the 60 trials) were each approximately 1 min in length.
evidence: The authors describe their experimental design.

claim: There were a total of 12 learning sweeps throughout the experiment.
source: There were a total of 12 learning sweeps throughout the experiment (divided into four scanning runs, or 'quarters', comprising three sweeps each).
evidence: The authors describe their experimental design.

claim: Each 3-sweep scanning run lasted 15–20 min.
source: Each 3-sweep scanning run lasted 15–20 min and subjects could take a short break (while remaining in the scanner) between scanning runs when necessary.
evidence: The authors describe their experimental procedure.

claim: A Bayesian implementation of a 'state-space' model provided the best fit to the learning data.
source: Of the models tested (see 'Materials and methods') a Bayesian implementation of a 'state-space' model provided the best fit to the data (Smith et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by model comparison analysis.

claim: T2*-weighted single-shot echo-planar images with BOLD contrast were acquired on a 3T Magnetom Allegra head-only MRI scanner.
source: T2*-weighted single-shot echo-planar images with BOLD contrast were acquired on a 3T Magnetom Allegra head-only MRI scanner (Siemens Healthcare, Erlangen, Germany) operated with the standard transmit-receive head coil.
evidence: The authors describe their scanning parameters.

claim: FMRI data were analysed using SPM8.
source: FMRI data were analysed using SPM8 (www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm).
evidence: The authors describe their analysis methods.
